extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for USPTO examiners on the standards for evaluating and entering affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 and 1.132, including timeliness, sufficiency, objective evidence of nonobviousness, and required factual support. Covers procedures, form paragraphs, evidentiary weight, and related statutory requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception is more than a mere vague idea of how to solve a problem; the means themselves and their interaction must be comprehended also.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites case law establishing that conception requires a complete mental picture of the invention and how it will be accomplished (e.g., In re Asahi/America Inc., Newkirk v. Lulejian). Use MPEP § 2138.04-2138.06 for detailed discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to Practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof of actual reduction to practice requires showing that the apparatus actually existed and worked for its intended purpose; for some simple devices, mere construction is sufficient to constitute reduction to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: photographs, articles, and technical reports describing the device in detail may suffice. See In re Asahi/America Inc. and cited cases for when mere construction is adequate. Reduction to practice may be actual or constructive (filing an application). See MPEP § 2138.04-2138.06.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and Scope of a 37 CFR 1.131 Affidavit
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of filing a 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit is not to demonstrate prior invention per se but merely to antedate the effective date of a reference; the sufficiency test parallels interference priority but 1.131 practice is not controlled strictly by interference law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court guidance (In re Eickmeyer, In re Moore, In re Borkowski) — the ‘conception’ and ‘reduction to practice’ required under Rule 131 need not be the same as in an interference. Also, averments in a 1.131 affidavit or declaration do not require corroboration; an applicant may stand on their own affidavit (Ex parte Hook).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of Utility under 1.131
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof of a utility is required only if the reference discloses a utility; whether test results are required depends on the facts of each case and whether one of ordinary skill would be satisfied to a reasonable certainty that the subject matter possessed the alleged utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Wilkinson, In re Moore, In re Blake. Examiner must evaluate whether evidence would satisfy one skilled in the art to a reasonable certainty that the invention had the alleged utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where conception occurs prior to the date of the reference but reduction to practice is afterward, applicant must show evidence establishing diligence; diligence is judged on the particular facts of each case and an inventor is either diligent at a given time or not (no degrees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record must set forth an explanation or excuse for inactivity; USPTO/courts will not speculate. Critical diligence period begins just prior to the effective date of the reference and ends with the date of reduction to practice (actual or constructive). Only diligence before reduction to practice is material; lapse of time after completion to filing is not relevant to 1.131 affidavits. See Ex parte Hunter, Christie v. Seybold, Ex parte Kantor, In re Nelson, Ex parte Merz, and MPEP § 2138.06.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Interference Testimony as Substitute Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony of the applicant in an interference may sometimes be used to antedate a reference in lieu of a 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit or declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part(s) of the testimony that form the basis of priority over the reference should be pointed out (Ex parte Bowyer). Use where appropriate to supplement or replace 1.131 evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic Limitations on Acts Relied Upon (35 U.S.C. 104)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts relied upon to establish a date prior to the reference or activity must have been carried out in the United States or in a NAFTA country or WTO member country; the 1.131 affidavit/declaration must contain an allegation to that effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines NAFTA/WTO timing: NAFTA acts on/after Dec 8, 1993 may establish completion in NAFTA country; WTO (other than NAFTA) on/after Jan 1, 1996. Acts occurring prior to those effective dates may be relied upon to show completion, but completion dates may not be established before those effective dates. See statutory text of 35 U.S.C. 104 and related MPEP discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition and Compliance of Exhibits (37 CFR 1.91)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhibits filed as part of an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 must comply with the requirements of 37 CFR 1.91 to be entered into an application file; noncomplying exhibits may be disposed of or returned to applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 608.03(a) for guidance on exhibit handling. Examiner discretion on disposition of noncompliant exhibits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary Examiner Review Responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of sufficiency of affidavits or declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 should be reviewed and decided by a primary examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary examiner must personally review and decide sufficiency; formal sufficiency/propriety issues are by petition (37 CFR 1.181) answered by Technology Center Directors; review on the merits is by appeal to the Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / Seasonable Presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits or declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 (and evidence traversing rejections) must be timely presented to be admitted; evidence is considered timely if submitted under specific conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely if: (A) prior to a final rejection; (B) before appeal in an application not having a final rejection; (C) after final rejection but before or on same date as filing an appeal upon a showing of good and sufficient reasons why it was not earlier presented; or (D) after prosecution is closed if submitted with a request for continued examination (RCE) or as CPA in a design application. All admitted affidavits/declarations are acknowledged and commented upon by the examiner in the next action. Review of refusal to enter as untimely is by petition, not appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review for Prior Public Use/On-Sale and Best Mode Risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must determine whether affidavits/declarations and accompanying evidence show that the claimed invention was in public use or on sale in the U.S. more than one year prior to the effective filing date (statutory bar), and whether the evidence indicates failure to disclose the best mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a reference is antedated, applicant's own prior public use/on-sale activities may create a statutory bar under 35 U.S.C. 102(b). If the 1.131 evidence relies on an embodiment not disclosed in the application, consider the best mode requirement and make a best-mode rejection only if preponderance of the evidence shows specification fails to set forth the best mode. See MPEP §§ 2133.03 and 2165-2165.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for Oath/Declaration Under 37 CFR 1.132
rubrics_metrics.description: When any claim of an application or a patent under reexamination is rejected or objected to, any evidence submitted to traverse the rejection or objection on a basis not otherwise provided for must be by way of an oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the general policy for receiving affidavit evidence traversing rejections or objections. All affidavits/declarations not falling under other specific rules are to be treated under this rule. Use form paragraphs 7.65 or 7.66 and subparagraphs 7.66.01–7.66.05 as appropriate to comment on a 1.132 affidavit or declaration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form Paragraph 7.65 — Affidavit/Declaration Effective to Withdraw Rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Template finding that the affidavit/declaration filed on [date] is sufficient to overcome the rejection of specified claim(s) based upon identified grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes examiner notes on inserting affidavit/declaration, filing date, affected claims, and the rejection overcome (statutory grounds) e.g., 35 U.S.C. 112, 101, 103, etc. Should be used when the evidence is sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form Paragraph 7.66 — Affidavit/Declaration Insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Template stating that the affidavit/declaration filed is insufficient to overcome the rejection of specified claim(s) based upon identified grounds, followed by reasons for insufficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must state specific reasons for insufficiency (e.g., untimely; fails to set forth facts; facts not germane to rejection; showing not commensurate in scope with claims) and include a detailed explanation. May employ form paragraphs 7.66.01–7.66.05 as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.66.01 — Affiant Has Never Seen the Invention (Insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavit includes statements amounting to an affirmation that the affiant has never seen the claimed subject matter before, which is not relevant to nonobviousness and provides no objective evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.66 and include a full explanation if appropriate. Cites MPEP § 716.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.66.02 — Invention Works as Intended (Insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavit includes statements that the claimed subject matter functions as intended, which is not relevant to nonobviousness and provides no objective evidence thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.66. Such affirmations do not establish nonobviousness. See MPEP § 716.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.66.03 — Refers Only to Invention, Not to Claims (Insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavit refers only to the system described in the application and not to the individual claims; does not show that objective evidence of nonobviousness is commensurate in scope with the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.66; provide full explanation if appropriate. Evidence must be commensurate in scope with the claims to be probative.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.66.04 — No Evidence of Long-Felt Need (Insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavit states the claimed subject matter solved a long-standing problem but provides no showing that others of ordinary skill were working on the problem or that knowledge of the cited references would not have enabled them to solve it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.66 and include a full explanation if appropriate. Mere assertion of long-felt need without evidence is insufficient (see MPEP § 716.04).

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.66.05 — Conclusion That Rebuttal Fails (Insufficient Conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concluding form paragraph that, when all evidence is considered, the totality of rebuttal evidence of nonobviousness fails to outweigh the evidence of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Should be presented as the conclusion to the explanation of why the affidavit/declaration is insufficient and must be preceded by form paragraph 7.66.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness as a Generally Applicable Criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Timeliness is a threshold criterion applicable to all evidence traversing rejections: evidence must be timely or seasonably filed to be entered and entitled to consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits/declarations under 1.132 follow the same timeliness rules as 1.131; see the enumerated timely submission conditions. In re Rothermel cited. If untimely, evidence may be refused entry and review of refusal is by petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration and Explanation of Evidence by Examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: When timely presented, evidence traversing rejections must be considered by the examiner and acknowledged and commented upon in the next action; comments should be specific and explain sufficiency or insufficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence overcomes prima facie case, comments should follow guidelines for reasons for allowance (MPEP § 1302.14). If insufficient, examiner must specifically explain why — general unsupported statements are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective Evidence of Nonobviousness Must Be Considered When Timely Presented
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits/declarations containing evidence of criticality or unexpected results, commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, skepticism of experts, etc., must be considered in determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Stratoflex, Graham v. John Deere, In re Palmer, In re Fielder and others. Comparative data in the specification intended to illustrate the claimed invention must be considered. Lack of objective evidence does not weigh in favor of obviousness, but failure to rebut a prima facie case can be dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus Requirement for Secondary Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: To be probative, any secondary (objective) evidence of nonobviousness must be related to the claimed invention — a factual and legally sufficient nexus is required between the evidence and the claimed merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must determine nexus before giving substantial weight to secondary considerations; cites Ashland Oil and Demaco case law for nexus concept and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probative Value — Requirement for Factual Support
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence should be supported by actual proof (e.g., comparative data, tests) to be of probative value for unexpected results, commercial success, long-felt need, inoperability of prior art, invention before the reference, or derivation allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re De Blauwe and other cases showing experimental data or comparative tests are necessary. Attorney argument cannot replace factual evidence (In re Schulze). Opinion evidence is admissible but limited: opinions not on ultimate legal conclusions and supported by facts may be given weight; consider expert interest and factual support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing Objective Evidence Against Prima Facie Case
rubrics_metrics.description: In making a final determination of patentability, evidence supporting patentability must be weighed against evidence supporting the examiner’s prima facie case; the ultimate determination is by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All competent rebuttal evidence taken as a whole should be weighed against the prima facie case (In re Piasecki). If examiner remains unconvinced, the next Office action must state reasons and identify why the rebuttal evidence failed to overcome the prima facie case; see MPEP § 2145 for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegations of Unexpected Results — Substantive Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Any differences between the claimed invention and the prior art may result in differences in properties; the key is whether the properties differ to such an extent that the difference is truly unexpected (a marked improvement or difference in kind rather than merely degree).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law examples: In re Merck & Co., In re Waymouth, In re Wagner, Ex parte Gelles. Evidence of greater-than-expected results (including synergism) can support nonobviousness, but applicants must show results greater than those expected from the prior art to an unobvious extent and that the results provide a significant, practical advantage. Greater-than-additive effects are not necessarily sufficient if such effects could have been expected.
